title: Administrative Order A-2017-033
content:
## First Appearance and Bond Timing

- Duty judges preside over first-appearance hearings and bond motions:
  - Via audiovisual devices.
  - From Courtroom 17, Courthouse Annex, Tampa, Florida.
- Timing:
  - **Non-holiday weekdays:** Commencing at **9:00 a.m.**
  - **Weekends and holidays:** Commencing **immediately after the juvenile detention and shelter hearings**.
- On non-holiday weekdays, duty judges also conduct criminal proceedings assigned to **First Appearance / Emergency Division “O.”**
- Duty judges are assigned for one-week periods:
  - Beginning at **9:00 a.m. on Monday**.
  - Ending at **8:59 a.m. the following Monday**.
- On non-holiday weekdays, duty judges are expected to remain at the courthouse until at least **5:00 p.m.**
- Duty judges must clear the morning dockets in their regularly assigned divisions to enable them to preside daily over first-appearance hearings and bond hearings.
- If a duty judge maintains an afternoon docket in a regularly assigned division, the judge must stop that work to accommodate duty-judge responsibilities that arise.

## Hillsborough First-Appearance Procedure and Location

| Proceeding | Location | Timing |
|---|---|---|
| First-appearance hearings and bond motions | Courtroom 17, Courthouse Annex, Tampa, Florida, via audiovisual devices | 9:00 a.m. on non-holiday weekdays; immediately after juvenile detention and shelter hearings on weekends and holidays |
| Juvenile detention and shelter hearings | Courtroom 16, Courthouse Annex, Tampa, Florida | 8:30 a.m. on weekends and holidays |

- On weekends and holidays, first-appearance hearings and bond motions occur after the juvenile detention and shelter hearings.
- The administrative order does not provide additional details about the audiovisual procedure, bond-motion filing procedure, courtroom access procedure, or hearing sequence beyond the information above.

## Limitations and Emergency-Matter Rules

- Duty judges consider emergency applications for extraordinary relief only when, under the established emergency procedures of the applicable subject-matter division, **no judge is present in the courthouse** to consider the application.
- The duty judge must determine:
  - Whether an emergency exists.
  - Whether requested relief is suitable for ex parte consideration if ex parte relief is requested.
  - Whether a hearing with notice to the adverse party is required under the applicable court rules.
- If the duty judge determines that no emergency exists or denies the emergency request without a hearing:
  - The requesting party may not present the request to another judge.
  - The request may be presented only to the division judge to whom the case is assigned, or, in an unassigned action, to the division judge to whom the case will be assigned.
- If the duty judge determines that the emergency requires an imminent return hearing, the duty judge conducts the return hearing personally.
- If the duty judge determines that a noticed hearing is required but that it need not occur imminently, the hearing is scheduled in:
  - The division where the case is pending; or
  - For an unassigned action, the division where the case will be pending.
- Duty judges consider emergency petitions for authorization for medical treatment when the assigned judge, chief judge, or chief judge’s designee is unavailable.
- Duty judges consider emergency petitions for appointment of a representative ad litem for organ-donation purposes when the assigned judge, chief judge, or chief judge’s designee is unavailable.
- The order states that duty judges are available after first-appearance hearings on weekdays and after hours on weekdays and holidays for applications involving:
  - Search warrants.
  - Arrest warrants.
  - Inspection warrants.
  - Agricultural warrants.
  - Wiretaps.
  - Pen registers.
  - Trap-and-trace devices.
  - Mobile tracking devices.
- The chief judge may assign duty judges to preside over juvenile detention hearings, shelter hearings, and other priority matters in addition to first-appearance hearings on non-holiday weekdays if court facilities are closed because of a hurricane or other emergency event.
- The chief judge may designate alternate or additional duty judges for those priority matters.
- The posted 2018 schedule states that it does not reflect changes between judges and directs readers to the Thirteenth Judicial Circuit website for an up-to-date schedule.

## Statutory and Holiday Caveats Stated in the Order

- **Section 26.20, Florida Statutes:** The order states that the statute requires at least one judge in circuits having more than one circuit judge to be available, as nearly as possible at all times, to hold and conduct hearings in chambers.
- The order also states that section 26.20 requires at least one judge to be available on Saturdays, Sundays, holidays, and after-hours on weekdays to consider ex parte petitions for temporary injunctions in domestic-violence cases.
- **Section 683.19, Florida Statutes:** The order states that the chief judge designated Good Friday, Rosh Hashanah, and Yom Kippur as legal holidays for the courts.
- Because the clerk’s office remains open on weekdays when those three holidays occur, the duty judge is assigned for the entire day to review Baker Act petitions on:
  - Good Friday, **March 30, 2018**.
  - Rosh Hashanah, **September 10, 2018**.
  - Yom Kippur, **September 19, 2018**.
- On those three holidays, the duty judge reviews petitions seeking an ex parte order requiring involuntary examination under the Florida Mental Health Act, identified in the order as the **Baker Act**.
- The order also identifies:
  - **Section 390.01114, Florida Statutes**, concerning petitions seeking a judicial waiver of abortion-notice requirements.
  - **Section 43.26, Florida Statutes**.
  - **Article V, section 2(d), Florida Constitution**.
  - **Florida Rule of Judicial Administration 2.215(b)(2)**.

## DUI Criminal Elements and Administrative Suspension or Review

- The page does **not** state the criminal elements of DUI.
- The page does **not** state DUI classification rules.
- The page does **not** state administrative driver-license suspension rules.
- The page does **not** state an administrative-suspension review deadline or timeline.
- The page does **not** state procedures for requesting or conducting an administrative review.

- The page does not provide felony-degree or misdemeanor-degree classifications, penalties, or charge-specific statutory citations.

## Criminal-prosecution limitation periods — Fla. Stat. § 775.15

### General rules

| Offense | Limitation period |
|---|---:|
| Capital felony | May be commenced at any time |
| Life felony | May be commenced at any time |
| Felony that resulted in a death | May be commenced at any time |
| First-degree felony | Within 4 years after commission |
| Any other felony | Within 3 years after commission |
| First-degree misdemeanor | Within 2 years after commission |
| Second-degree misdemeanor or noncriminal violation | Within 1 year after commission |

- If the death penalty is held unconstitutional by the Florida Supreme Court or the United States Supreme Court, all crimes designated as capital felonies are considered life felonies for purposes of this section, and prosecution may be commenced at any time.
- The general periods apply “[e]xcept as otherwise provided in this section.”
- An offense is committed:
  - When every element has occurred; or
  - If a legislative purpose to prohibit a continuing course of conduct plainly appears, when the course of conduct or the defendant’s complicity in it is terminated.
- Time begins to run on the day after the offense is committed.

### When prosecution is commenced

- If the defendant has previously been arrested or served with a summons, prosecution on the charge is commenced by filing an indictment, information, or other charging document.
- If the defendant has not previously been arrested or served with a summons, prosecution is commenced when an indictment or information is filed, provided that the capias, summons, or other process issued on the indictment or information is executed without unreasonable delay.
- In determining what constitutes reasonable delay, the following must be considered:
  - Inability to locate the defendant after diligent search.
  - The defendant’s absence from the state.
- Failure to execute process on, or extradite, a defendant in another state who has been charged by information or indictment with a crime in Florida does not constitute unreasonable delay.
- If an indictment or information is filed within the prescribed limitation period but is later dismissed or set aside because of a defect in its content or form after the period has elapsed, the period for commencing prosecution is extended 3 months from the time the indictment or information is dismissed or set aside.

### Absence from Florida or lack of ascertainable residence or employment

- The limitation period does not run while the defendant:
  - Is continuously absent from Florida; or
  - Has no reasonably ascertainable place of abode or work within Florida.
- This provision cannot extend the otherwise applicable limitation period by more than 3 years.
- It does not limit prosecution of a defendant who:
  - Was timely charged by indictment, information, or other charging document; and
  - Has not been arrested because of absence from Florida or has not been extradited for prosecution from another state.

### Offenses with special limitation periods

| Offense or statutory provision | Limitation rule |
|---|---|
| Perjury in an official proceeding relating to prosecution of a capital felony | May be commenced at any time |
| Felony resulting in injury to any person and arising from use of a “destructive device” as defined in § 790.001 | Within 10 years |
| Felony violation of Chapter 517 or § 409.920 | Within 5 years after the violation is committed |
| Felony violation of Chapter 403 | Within 5 years after discovery of the violation |
| Felony violation of § 817.5695, § 825.102, or § 825.103 | Within 5 years after commission |
| Felony violation of § 440.105 or § 817.234 | Within 5 years after commission |
| Misdemeanor violation of § 784.049 | Within 5 years after commission or within 3 years after the victim discovers the offense, whichever is later |
| Felony violation of § 784.049 | Within 7 years after commission or within 3 years after the victim discovers the offense, whichever is later |
| Violation of § 787.06 | May be commenced at any time, subject to the stated prior-bar caveat |
| Violation of § 39.201 | The limitation period does not begin until a law-enforcement agency or other governmental agency, excluding an institution where the violation occurs, is made aware of the violation |

For a felony violation of § 817.5695, § 825.102, or § 825.103:

- If the applicable 5-year period has expired, prosecution may nevertheless be commenced for an offense whose material element is fraud or breach of fiduciary obligation:
  - Within 5 years after discovery of the offense by an aggrieved party; or
  - Within 5 years after discovery by a person who has a legal duty to represent an aggrieved party and who is not a party to the offense.

### Fraud, breach of fiduciary obligation, and misconduct in office

If the limitation period under subsection (2), (8), (9), (10), or (11) has expired, prosecution may nevertheless be commenced for:

- An offense whose material element is fraud or breach of fiduciary obligation:
  - Within 1 year after discovery by an aggrieved party; or
  - Within 1 year after discovery by a person who has a legal duty to represent an aggrieved party and who is not a party to the offense.
  - This provision may not extend the otherwise applicable limitation period by more than 3 years.
- An offense based on misconduct in office by a public officer or employee:
  - At any time while the defendant is in public office or employment;
  - Within 2 years after the defendant leaves public office or employment; or
  - During any time permitted by another part of § 775.15,
  - Whichever time is greater.

### Sexual offenses involving victims under 18

For a violation of § 794.011, former § 794.05, Florida Statutes 1995, § 800.04, § 826.04, or § 847.0135(5), when the victim is under 18:

- The applicable limitation period does not begin until the victim:
  - Reaches age 18; or
  - Reports the violation to a law-enforcement agency or other governmental agency,
  - Whichever occurs earlier.
- The agency receiving the allegation must promptly report it to the state attorney for the judicial circuit in which the alleged violation occurred.
- If the offense is a first- or second-degree felony violation of § 794.011 and is reported within 72 hours after commission, prosecution may be commenced at any time.
- This paragraph applies except to an offense that would have been barred under subsection (2) on or before December 31, 1984.

Additional rules for § 794.011:

- A first-degree felony violation may be prosecuted at any time when the victim was under 18 at the time of the offense.
  - This applies except to an offense that would have been barred under subsection (2) on or before October 1, 2003.
- A violation may be prosecuted at any time when the victim was under 16 at the time of the offense.
  - This applies except to an offense that would have been barred under subsection (2) on or before July 1, 2010.
- If the victim was younger than 18 at the time of the offense, a prosecution may be commenced at any time.
  - This applies to offenses committed on or after July 1, 2020.

For first- or second-degree felony violations of § 794.011 when the victim was 16 or older:

- If the offense is reported to a law-enforcement agency within 72 hours after commission, prosecution may be commenced at any time.
- Except as provided in that rule or the rule for victims under 18, prosecution must be commenced within 8 years after commission.
- The 8-year rule applies except to an offense that would have been barred under subsection (2) on or before July 1, 2015.

### DNA-based identification

In addition to the otherwise applicable periods, prosecution may be commenced within 1 year after the date on which the accused’s identity is established, or should have been established through due diligence, through DNA analysis, if:

- A sufficient portion of the evidence collected during the original investigation and tested for DNA is preserved; and
- The evidence is available for testing by the accused.

The 1-year DNA rule applies to:

1. An offense of sexual battery under Chapter 794.
2. A lewd or lascivious offense under § 800.04 or § 825.1025.

- This subsection applies to an offense that was not otherwise barred from prosecution between July 1, 2004, and June 30, 2006.

For the following offenses, prosecution may be commenced at any time after the accused’s identity is established, or should have been established through due diligence, through DNA analysis, if the same evidence-preservation and availability conditions are met:

1. Aggravated battery or any felony battery offense under Chapter 784.
2. Kidnapping under § 787.01 or false imprisonment under § 787.02.
3. An offense of sexual battery under Chapter 794.
4. A lewd or lascivious offense under § 800.04, § 825.1025, or § 847.0135(5).
5. A burglary offense under § 810.02.
6. A robbery offense under § 812.13, § 812.131, or § 812.135.
7. Carjacking under § 812.133.
8. Aggravated child abuse under § 827.03.

- This any-time DNA rule applies to an offense that was not otherwise barred from prosecution on or after July 1, 2006.

### Digital voyeurism

- A prosecution for digital voyeurism under § 810.145 may be commenced within 1 year after whichever occurs first:
  - The victim obtains actual knowledge of the existence of the recording; or
  - The recording is confiscated by a law-enforcement agency.
- Dissemination of the recording before the victim obtains actual knowledge or before confiscation does not affect any provision of this subsection.

### Lewd or lascivious offenses involving victims under 16

- If the offense is a violation of § 800.04(4) or (5) and the victim was under 16 at the time of the offense, prosecution may be commenced at any time.
- Exception: this does not apply when, at the time of the offense:
  - The offender was under 18; and
  - The offender was no more than 4 years older than the victim.
- This applies to an offense not otherwise barred from prosecution on or before October 1, 2014.

### Commercial sexual exploitation of children

- A prosecution for an offense under § 827.071(2) or (3) may be commenced at any time if the offender was 18 or older at the time of the offense.
- This applies to an offense not otherwise barred from prosecution on or before July 1, 2022.

### Failure to report child abuse

- For a violation of § 39.201, the applicable limitation period does not begin until a law-enforcement agency or other governmental agency is made aware of the violation.
- An institution where the violation occurs is excluded from the agencies whose awareness starts the period.
- This applies to an offense not otherwise barred from prosecution on or before July 1, 2026.

## Limitations

## DUI Criminal Rules

- The page content refers to a violation of subsection (1), but does not set out the DUI criminal elements.
- For purposes of the referenced subsection:
  - Only the instant offense is required to be a violation of subsection (1) by a person with a blood-alcohol level or breath-alcohol level of **0.15 or higher**.
  - The portion of a fine exceeding **$1,000** imposed under subparagraph (a)1. must be remitted by the clerk to the Department of Revenue for deposit into the General Revenue Fund.
  - The portion of a fine exceeding **$2,000** imposed under subparagraph (a)2. or subparagraph (a)3. must be remitted by the clerk to the Department of Revenue for deposit into the General Revenue Fund.
- A person convicted of DUI manslaughter must receive a mandatory minimum term of imprisonment of **4 years**.
- For purposes of the subsection, “unborn child” has the same meaning as provided in **s. 775.021(5)**.

## Administrative Suspension and Review Timeline

- The page content does not state the administrative-suspension process or any review timeline.

## Previous Convictions Treated as Prior Violations

The following are considered previous convictions for violation of the section:

- Any conviction for a violation of **s. 327.35**.
- A previous conviction under:
  - Former **s. 316.1931**.
  - Former **s. 860.01**.
  - Former **s. 316.028**.
- A previous conviction outside Florida for:
  - Driving under the influence.
  - Driving while intoxicated.
  - Driving with an unlawful blood-alcohol level.
  - Driving with an unlawful breath-alcohol level.
  - Any other similar alcohol-related or drug-related traffic offense.

## Fine-Related Rules

- The portion of a fine exceeding **$500** imposed pursuant to sub-subparagraph 1.a. must be remitted by the clerk to the Department of Revenue for deposit into the General Revenue Fund.
- The portion of a fine exceeding **$1,000** imposed pursuant to sub-subparagraph 1.b. must be remitted by the clerk to the Department of Revenue for deposit into the General Revenue Fund.
- If the court finds that the defendant is financially unable to pay all or part of the fine, the court may order the defendant to participate for a specified additional period in:
  - Public service; or
  - A community work project.
- The public service or community work project may be ordered in lieu of payment of the portion of the fine the court determines the defendant cannot pay.
- In determining the additional sentence, the court must consider:
  - The amount of the unpaid portion of the fine.
  - The reasonable value of the services ordered.
- The court may not calculate the reasonable value of the services at a rate less than the federal minimum wage in effect at the time of sentencing.

## DUI-Related Administrative Suspension Rules

### Grounds for suspension

A law enforcement officer or correctional officer shall, on behalf of the Department of Highway Safety and Motor Vehicles, suspend the driving privilege of a person who:

- Is driving or in actual physical control of a motor vehicle and has:
  - An unlawful blood-alcohol level of **0.08 or higher**; or
  - An unlawful breath-alcohol level of **0.08 or higher**; or
- Refuses to submit to:
  - A urine test;
  - A breath-alcohol test; or
  - A blood-alcohol test.

The officer shall:

- Take the person’s driver license;
- Issue a **10-day temporary permit** if the person is otherwise eligible for the driving privilege; and
- Issue a notice of suspension.

If a blood test was administered:

- The officer or the agency employing the officer shall transmit the results to the Department within **5 days after receipt**.
- If the Department determines that the person had a blood-alcohol level or breath-alcohol level of **0.08 or higher**, the Department shall suspend the driver license under subsection (3).

### Suspension periods stated in the notice

| Basis for suspension | First occurrence | Prior suspension under the applicable provision |
|---|---:|---:|
| Refusal to submit to a lawful breath, blood, or urine test | **1 year** | **18 months** if the driving privilege was previously suspended as a result of a refusal |
| Driving or actual physical control with an unlawful blood-alcohol level or breath-alcohol level of **0.08 or higher** | **6 months** | **1 year** if the driving privilege was previously suspended under this section |

- The suspension period begins on the date the notice of suspension is issued.
- The driver may request:
  - A formal review;
  - An informal review; or
  - A review of eligibility for a restricted driving privilege under s. 322.271(7).
- The request must be made within **10 days after the date of issuance of the notice of suspension**.
- The driver may submit materials relevant to the suspension to the Department.
- The temporary permit issued at suspension expires at **midnight of the 10th day following** the date the notice of suspension was issued.

### Materials forwarded to the Department

Except as provided in paragraph (1)(a), the law enforcement officer shall forward to the Department within **5 days after issuing the notice of suspension**:

- The driver license;
- An affidavit stating the officer’s grounds for believing that the person was driving or in actual physical control of a motor vehicle while under the influence of alcoholic beverages or chemical or controlled substances;
- The results of any breath or blood test, or an affidavit stating that a breath, blood, or urine test was requested by a law enforcement officer or correctional officer and that the person refused to submit;
- The officer’s description of the person’s field sobriety test, if any; and
- The notice of suspension.

Additional materials the officer may submit include:

- A copy of the crash report; and
- A copy of a video recording of the field sobriety test or the attempt to administer the test.

Additional statutory rules regarding submitted materials:

- The failure to submit materials within the specified 5-day period does not affect the Department’s ability to consider evidence submitted at or before the hearing.
- Materials submitted by a law enforcement agency or correctional agency are considered self-authenticating and are placed in the record for consideration by the hearing officer.
- Notwithstanding s. 316.066(4), the crash report shall be considered by the hearing officer.

### Department-issued notice and temporary permit

If the Department determines that the license should be suspended and the suspension notice has not already been served by a law enforcement officer or correctional officer:

- The Department shall issue a notice of suspension.
- Unless the notice is provided under s. 322.251, the Department shall issue a temporary permit expiring **10 days after issuance**, if the driver is otherwise eligible.

## Informal Review

- An informal review is conducted by a Department-designated hearing officer.
- The review consists solely of the Department’s examination of materials submitted by:
  - A law enforcement officer or correctional officer; and
  - The person whose license was suspended.
- The presence of an officer or witness is not required.
- After the informal review, notice of the Department’s decision to sustain, amend, or invalidate the suspension must be provided to the person.
- The notice must be:
  - Mailed to the last known address shown in the Department’s records;
  - Mailed to the address provided in the law enforcement officer’s report if it differs from the address of record; or
  - E-mailed to an e-mail address furnished to the Department.
- The notice must be sent within **21 days after the expiration of the temporary permit** issued under subsection (1) or subsection (3).

## Formal Review

### Scheduling and notice

- If the person requests a formal review, the Department must schedule a hearing within **30 days after receiving the request**.
- The Department must notify the person of the hearing’s:
  - Date;
  - Time; and
  - Place.

### Hearing officer’s authority

The formal review is held before a Department-designated hearing officer. The hearing officer may:

- Administer oaths;
- Examine witnesses;
- Take testimony;
- Receive relevant evidence;
- Issue subpoenas for officers and witnesses identified in the materials submitted under paragraph (2)(a);
- Regulate the course and conduct of the hearing;
- Question witnesses; and
- Rule on the suspension.

The hearing officer may conduct hearings using communications technology.

Additional procedural rules:

- The party requesting a witness’s presence is responsible for:
  - Paying any witness fees; and
  - Notifying in writing the state attorney’s office in the appropriate circuit of the subpoena’s issuance.
- If the person requesting a formal review fails to appear and the hearing officer finds that the failure was without just cause:
  - The right to a formal hearing is waived; and
  - The suspension shall be sustained.
- The failure of a subpoenaed witness to appear is not grounds to invalidate the suspension.
- A party may seek subpoena enforcement by:
  - Filing a petition for enforcement in the circuit court of the judicial circuit where the noncomplying person resides; or
  - Filing a motion for enforcement in any criminal court case arising from the driving or actual physical control that gave rise to the suspension.
- Failure to comply with a court order results in a finding of contempt of court.
- A person is not in contempt while challenging a subpoena.
- Within **7 working days after the formal review hearing**, the Department must send notice of the hearing officer’s decision regarding whether sufficient cause exists to sustain, amend, or invalidate the suspension.

### Formal review based on reports

- A formal review may be conducted based on law enforcement or correctional officer reports, including documents concerning:
  - Administration of a breath test;
  - Administration of a blood test;
  - Refusal to take a breath test;
  - Refusal to take a blood test; or
  - Refusal to take a urine test.
- The driver may subpoena:
  - The officer; or
  - Any person who administered or analyzed a breath or blood test.
- If the arresting officer or breath technician fails to appear after being subpoenaed as provided in subsection (6), the Department shall invalidate the suspension.

## Issues Considered at Review

At either a formal review or an informal review, the hearing officer determines by a **preponderance of the evidence** whether sufficient cause exists to sustain, amend, or invalidate the suspension.

The review is limited to the following issues.

### Suspension based on an unlawful alcohol level

The hearing officer considers:

1. Whether the law enforcement officer had probable cause to believe that the person was driving or in actual physical control of a motor vehicle in Florida while under the influence of:
   - Alcoholic beverages; or
   - Chemical or controlled substances.
2. Whether the person had an unlawful blood-alcohol level or breath-alcohol level of **0.08 or higher**, as provided in s. 316.193.

### Suspension based on refusal

The hearing officer considers:

1. Whether the law enforcement officer had probable cause to believe that the person was driving or in actual physical control of a motor vehicle in Florida while under the influence of:
   - Alcoholic beverages; or
   - Chemical or controlled substances.
2. Whether the person refused to submit to a breath, blood, or urine test after being requested to do so by a law enforcement officer or correctional officer.
3. Whether the person was told that refusal would result in suspension of the privilege to operate a motor vehicle for:
   - **1 year**; or
   - **18 months** in the case of a second or subsequent refusal.

## Effect of Review and Suspension Periods

Based on the hearing officer’s determination:

- For a refusal to submit to a lawful breath, blood, or urine test:
  - The Department shall sustain a suspension for **1 year** for a first refusal.
  - The Department shall sustain a suspension for **18 months** if the person’s driving privilege was previously suspended because of a refusal.
- For an unlawful blood-alcohol level or breath-alcohol level of **0.08 or higher**:
  - The Department shall sustain a suspension for **6 months**.
  - The Department shall sustain a suspension for **1 year** if the person’s driving privilege was previously suspended under this section as a result of driving with an unlawful alcohol level.
- The suspension period begins on the date the notice of suspension is issued.

## Effect of Review Requests and Hearing Delays

- A request for a formal or informal review does **not** stay the driver license suspension.
- If the Department fails to schedule a formal review within **30 days after receiving the request**, the Department shall invalidate the suspension.
- If the scheduled hearing is continued:
  - At the Department’s initiative; or
  - Because the driver enforces a subpoena under subsection (6),
  
  the Department shall issue a temporary driving permit valid until the hearing is conducted, if the person is otherwise eligible.

- The temporary permit:
  - May not be issued to a person who sought and obtained a continuance of the hearing; and
  - Authorizes driving for **business or employment use only**.

## Business or Employment-Only License Eligibility

A person whose license is suspended under subsection (1) or subsection (3) may apply for a business- or employment-purpose-only license if otherwise eligible under s. 322.271.

### Refusal suspension

If the suspension for failure to submit to a breath, urine, or blood test is sustained:

- The person is not eligible for a business- or employment-purpose-only license until **90 days have elapsed after the expiration of the last temporary permit issued**.
- If the person was not issued a 10-day permit under this section or s. 322.64 because the person was ineligible for the permit, and the suspension is not invalidated by the Department, the person is not eligible until **90 days have elapsed from the date of suspension**.

### Unlawful alcohol-level suspension

If the suspension relating to an unlawful blood-alcohol level or breath-alcohol level of **0.08 or higher** is sustained:

- The person is not eligible for a business- or employment-purpose-only license until **30 days have elapsed after the expiration of the last temporary permit issued**.
- If the person was not issued a 10-day permit under this section or s. 322.64 because the person was ineligible for the permit, and the suspension is not invalidated by the Department, the person is not eligible until **30 days have elapsed from the date of suspension**.

## Appeals and Statutory Limitations

- A person may appeal a Department decision sustaining a suspension by petition for writ of certiorari to the circuit court in:
  - The county where the person resides; or
  - The county where the formal or informal review was conducted.
- An appeal does **not** stay the suspension.
- A law enforcement agency may appeal a Department decision invalidating a suspension by petition for writ of certiorari to the circuit court in the county where the formal or informal review was conducted.
- The appeal provision does not provide for a de novo review.
- Formal and informal review hearings are exempt from chapter 120.
- The Department may adopt rules governing reviews under this section.

## Relationship to Criminal DUI Proceedings

The page expressly states:

- The Department’s decision under this section, and any circuit court review of that decision, may not be considered in a trial for a violation of s. 316.193.
- A written statement submitted by a person in a request for Department review may not be admitted against that person in a trial for a violation of s. 316.193.
- The disposition of related criminal proceedings does not affect a suspension imposed under this section for refusing to submit to a blood, breath, or urine test.
- If the Department suspends a person’s license under s. 322.2616, it may not also suspend the license under this section for the same episode that formed the basis for the suspension under s. 322.2616.
- The Department shall invalidate a suspension imposed under this section for driving with an unlawful blood-alcohol level or breath-alcohol level if the person is found not guilty at trial of the underlying violation of s. 316.193.

## DUI Criminal Elements

The page does not provide the complete criminal elements or offense definitions under s. 316.193. It expressly identifies only the following matters relevant to the administrative review:

- Driving or being in actual physical control of a motor vehicle in Florida;
- Probable cause to believe the person was under the influence of alcoholic beverages or chemical or controlled substances;
- Having an unlawful blood-alcohol level or breath-alcohol level of **0.08 or higher**; and
- For refusal suspensions, refusing to submit to a requested breath, blood, or urine test after being requested to do so by a law enforcement officer or correctional officer.

## Florida Statutes § 775.08 — Classes and Definitions of Offenses

**The 2026 Florida Statutes**  
**Title XLVI — Crimes**  
**Chapter 775 — General Penalties; Registration of Criminals**

### Felony

- A “felony” means any criminal offense punishable under Florida law—or that would be punishable if committed in Florida—by:
  - Death; or
  - Imprisonment in a state penitentiary.
- “State penitentiary” includes state correctional facilities.
- A person is imprisoned in the state penitentiary for each sentence that, except for an extended term, exceeds 1 year.

### Misdemeanor

- A “misdemeanor” means any criminal offense punishable under Florida law—or that would be punishable if committed in Florida—by a term of imprisonment in a county correctional facility that, except for an extended term, does not exceed 1 year.
- “Misdemeanor” does not include:
  - A conviction for any noncriminal traffic violation of any provision of chapter 316; or
  - A conviction for any noncriminal traffic violation of any municipal or county ordinance.

### Noncriminal Violation

- A “noncriminal violation” means an offense punishable under Florida law—or that would be punishable if committed in Florida—by no penalty other than:
  - A fine;
  - Forfeiture; or
  - Another civil penalty.
- A noncriminal violation:
  - Does not constitute a crime; and
  - Does not, upon conviction, give rise to any legal disability based on a criminal offense.
- “Noncriminal violation” does not include any conviction for a violation of any municipal or county ordinance.
- Nothing in the Florida Criminal Code repeals or changes the penalty for a violation of any municipal or county ordinance.

### Crime

- A “crime” means a felony or misdemeanor.

## Battery: criminal elements and classifications

**Florida Statutes § 784.03, “Battery; felony battery”**

### Battery offense

The offense of battery occurs when a person:

1. Actually and intentionally touches or strikes another person against the will of the other; or
2. Intentionally causes bodily harm to another person.

### First-degree misdemeanor battery

Except as provided in subsection (2) or subsection (3), a person who commits battery commits a misdemeanor of the first degree, punishable as provided in:

- § 775.082; or
- § 775.083.

### Felony battery based on a prior conviction

A person who:

- Has one prior conviction for:
  - Battery;
  - Aggravated battery;
  - Felony battery; or
  - Resisting an officer with violence under § 843.01; and
- Commits any second or subsequent battery,

commits a felony of the third degree, punishable as provided in:

- § 775.082;
- § 775.083; or
- § 775.084.

For purposes of this subsection, “conviction” means a determination of guilt that is the result of a plea or a trial, regardless of whether:

- Adjudication is withheld; or
- A plea of nolo contendere is entered.

### Battery in furtherance of a riot or aggravated riot

A person who commits a battery in furtherance of a riot or an aggravated riot prohibited under § 870.01 commits a felony of the third degree, punishable as provided in:

- § 775.082;
- § 775.083; or
- § 775.084.

## Felony versus misdemeanor classifications for other common charges

- Not stated on the provided page.
- The page specifically states that ordinary battery, subject to the statutory exceptions, is a **misdemeanor of the first degree**.
- The page specifically states that battery by a person with the specified prior conviction, or battery committed in furtherance of a riot or aggravated riot, is a **felony of the third degree**.
